title: tail-latency-attribution-ebpf-pcie-clock-throttle-bench
body:
Summary:

This is a working note for an experiment that tries to attribute rare tail latency spikes (p95-p999) observed in our hosted API to low-level system events across different cloud GPU SKUs (A100/H100/L40S) and driver/CUDA stacks. Instead of the usual kernel-bench + nvprof approach we used previously, this run uses lightweight eBPF probes (tracepoints/kprobes) plus correlated telemetry (nvidia-smi sampling, PCIe counters, and perf) to link GPU clock/thermals, PCIe reset/flow-control events, and kernel preemption/softirqs to request-level latency anomalies.

Why this test?
- We keep seeing tail spikes that are not explained by batch packing statistics or KV warmups.
- Prior experiments pointed at transient host-induced stalls but could not correlate to GPU-side throttling or PCIe hiccups.
- eBPF lets us capture short-lived kernel events with millisecond timestamps without heavy perturbation.

Hypothesis:
1) Rare p99+/p999 spikes are often caused by transient GPU clock throttling (power/thermal or driver-driven) that coincides with brief host-side interrupts or PCIe bus stalls.
2) Different cloud SKUs and their host NIC/root-complex configurations produce different distributions of these events; newer platforms (L40S) show fewer PCIe flow-control stalls but may still throttle clocks under specific driver combos.
3) Certain CUDA/driver versions expose a pathological interaction between the kernel power-management callbacks and the RDMA/ethernet stack under bursty RPC patterns.

Test matrix (high level):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 (80GB), H100 (80GB), L40S (48GB)
- Instance SKUs: compact examples across three clouds (GCP + AWS + Azure regional equivalents) to capture different root-complex/NIC layouts
- Drivers/CUDA: pairings: (nvidia-driver 535 + CUDA 12.2), (nvidia-driver 525 + CUDA 11.8), (nvidia-driver 555 preview + CUDA 12.3) — chosen because customer fleet has these variants live
- Workloads: 1) 7B chat-style (seq 2048 prefill + 1024 decode) single-request microburst, 2) 70B prefills with small simultaneous background embedding traffic to simulate noisy co-tenancy, 3) short-turn chat (prefill 512 + decode 128) at small-batch (1–4) to stress tail latency
- Arrival patterns: Poisson baseline + engineered microburst (sudden 30 concurrent prefill requests) repeated every 5 minutes to elicit transient platform reactions

Instrumentation and sampling strategy:
- eBPF probes using the local test harness to collect:
  - kprobe:gpu_ioctl (capture driver ioctl paths and durations)
  - tracepoint:netif_receive_skb and kprobe:__netif_rx (to capture NIC softirq bursts)
  - perf sample attached to the process thread handling RPCs (call stacks, context-switches) at 1 kHz during bursts
  - tracepoint:pci_dev_runtime_resume/pci_dev_runtime_suspend to catch PCIe runtime power transitions
- nvidia-smi sampling at 100ms for GPU clocks, power draw, SM/util, and ECC errors; also poll nv-hostengine logs when available
- PCIe counters from ethtool and vendor sysfs where available (flow-control, retries) polled at 100ms during bursts
- Request-level tracing: include a unique trace-id injected into each request and recorded at the RPC entry, kernel timestamp, and model decode completion. This lets us compute precise delta between kernel events and observed latency spikes

Data collection notes:
- To minimize measurement perturbation, eBPF maps were kept small (per-cpu buffers flushed to userspace) and sampling toggled only during engineered microbursts.
- Tests ran for 6h per SKU/driver pairing with microbursts every 5min (72 microbursts) to accumulate rare-event statistics.
- We deliberately did not isolate NICs or change BIOS power settings; goal was to observe platform-as-provisioned behavior

Results (high-level observations):
- A100 (older hosts) + driver 525/CUDA11.8: frequent short-lived p99 spikes (~5–15ms extra) correlated with NIC softirq storms; eBPF tracepoints showed bursts of netif_receive_skb handling overlapping with GPU ioctl durations. PCIe counters showed increased retransmit/retry events during a subset (~12%) of spikes. Closer inspection: kernel logged occasional PCIe DPC (downstream port change) warnings on 3 occurrences across 6h.
- H100 hosts + driver 535/CUDA12.2: fewer NIC softirq overlaps; however, 2 clear p999 spikes (50–120ms) correlated with GPU clock downscaling events recorded by nvidia-smi (SM clock drop from 1.2GHz -> 300MHz for ~80–200ms) accompanied by a driver log "thermal mitigation" entry. These occurred under mixed background embedding traffic.
- L40S + driver 555/CUDA12.3 (preview): lowest overall p95, but saw rare PCIe runtime-suspend/resume events triggered concurrently with host-side PCIe error recovery paths. When those fires, request latency jumped by 100–300ms. Vendor sysfs showed link_recovery_count increments. Not reproducible on every microburst — seems conditioned on background DMA patterns.

Example attribution traces (text excerpt):
- trace-id=abc123: request start 12:01:05.233; kernel softirq burst start 12:01:05.237; gpu_ioctl blocked 12:01:05.239-12:01:05.341; nvidia-smi recorded SM clock drop at 12:01:05.240; rpc completion 12:01:05.440. Net delta = 207ms; eBPF shows concurrent kprobe on net driver path.

Preliminary conclusions:
- Tail spikes are multi-causal; different SKUs show different dominant failure modes: A100 hosts skew toward NIC/PCIe retries during heavy softirq; H100 shows genuine GPU thermal/power mitigation in a few cases; L40S shows PCIe runtime suspend interactions under odd DMA patterns.
- Driver/CUDA version matters: the 555 preview introduced a different runtime-suspend behavior (observed in logs) that amplified link recovery occurrences on certain host firmware.
- eBPF+trace correlates are effective: we can tie request trace-ids to kernel/driver events with millisecond granularity which allows targeted mitigations rather than gross timeouts or increasing SLOs

Quick mitigations to try (short-term):
- Add a small jitter to background embedding traffic to avoid synchronized DMA bursts causing PCIe flow-control on L40S hosts
- For H100 fleets, pin power-management mode to "Prefer Maximum Performance" where customers require strict tail SLOs, or add a runtime guard that falls back to a CPU-based short decode path if the GPU reports clock drops during prefill
- Update driver on a canary pool (555->stable) and instrument to see if runtime-suspend events decline

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Are the PCIe link_recovery_count increments always accompanied by CRC/retry counters at the NIC level? Need to collect vendor NIC counters in a follow-up run
- Can we reproduce the H100 thermal mitigation in a controlled lab with instrumented thermal sensors and synthetic power draw?
- What is the contribution of host BIOS/firmware revision? The three clouds had different base firmware; we should do a focused firmware sweep on one SKU (A100) to isolate this variable
- Longer runs to estimate p999 frequency: 6h yielded only a few p999 examples for each pairing; need 24–48h on a small canary pool to determine baseline frequencies

Notes to self / experiment log:
- harness branch: runtime/ebpf-tail-attrib (see linked PR)
- sampling knobs: eBPF buffer 4MB, perf sampling ramped to 1kHz only during bursts
- observed odd nv-hostengine message on H100: "nvhost_pm: invalid request state" — file logs in GH issue
- TODO: add NIC vendor counters (Mellanox/Intel) to next-run telemetry; instrument RDMA verbs counters where applicable

Appendix (quick commands used):
- eBPF probe loader: sudo ./probe_loader --map-size 4M --filters microburst
- nvidia sampling script: python tools/sample_nvidia.py --interval 0.1 --fields clocks,sm_util,power,temperature
- quick perf snapshot (during spike): sudo perf record -F 1000 -a -g -- sleep 1 && sudo perf script > spike.perf.txt

If useful, I can extract a few representative trace-ids and sanitized perf stacks and drop them into the Confluence playbook for on-call debugging.

Status: draft — want feedback from SRE and platform-firmware owners before we run the 48h follow-up.
summary_plain: Working doc describing eBPF-driven attribution experiments to map p95-p999 tail latency spikes to kernel/PCIe/GPU clock events across A100/H100/L40S and multiple driver/CUDA stacks. Includes hypothesis, test matrix, sampling strategy, results, preliminary mitigations, and follow-ups.
